newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia gold tax seen hurting state coffers.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia gold tax seen hurting state coffers.

text.p: A proposed gold royalty tax in Western Australia would cost five times as much as it raises, according to a study released on Monday by an industry group.

Based on the current spot gold price, a 2.5 percent royalty being considered by the state government of Western Australia would raise A$75 million a year, the Chamber of Minerals and Energy of Western Australia said.

However, this would decline to around A$50 million a year on a net basis, taking into account reductions in government revenue from payroll tax and fuel levies, the chamber said, citing an independent study by the Economic Research Centre of the University of Western Australia.

The loss to the state's economy would be A$100 million almost immediately, rising to A$250 million a year in five years due to the impact on gold exports, mine supply companies and employment levels, the chamber said.
The royalty also would result in the loss of about 1,450 jobs statewide, the study said.

Western Australia state premier Richard Court has said the state's proposal was to introduce a royalty of 1.25 percent of gold sale proceeds from January 1 next year, rising to 2.5 percent by July 1999, to compensate for cuts in federal funding.
Western Australia produces about 70 percent of Australia's annual gold production of nearly 300 tonnes.
Unlike miners in other states, gold miners in Western Australia currently are exempt from paying royalties on gold although other metals are subject to royalties in that state.
Queensland has a 2.75 percent gross royalty, while in New South Wales a net smelter levy of four percent is equal to about a two percent gross royalty.
The Northern Territory has an 18 percent net profit royalty.
